titleStmt.title: Shiji 史记 · 秦庄襄王元年

bibl.title: 无骨者伊瓦尔《战国历史地图·年表》

div.head: Shiji I: Basic Annals
div.p: Basic Annals of Zhou: Seven years later, King Zhuangxiang of Qin destroyed Eastern Zhou. Eastern and Western Zhou both passed into Qin's hands, and Zhou's sacrifices ended altogether.

Basic Annals of Qin: In the first year of King Zhuangxiang, he granted a great pardon to offenders, honoured the meritorious servants of the former kings, showed favour and generosity to his kin, and spread his bounty among the people. The Lord of Eastern Zhou plotted against Qin with the Lords; Qin sent the Chancellor of State Lü Buwei to punish him and took in the whole of his state. Qin did not cut off his sacrifices: it granted the Lord of Zhou the land of Yangren so that he might keep up his sacrifices. It sent Meng Ao to attack Han, and Han presented Chenggao and Gong. Qin's border reached to Daliang, and for the first time Sanchuan Commandery was established.

div.head: Shiji II: Tables
div.p: Qin: Meng Ao took Chenggao and Xingyang; Sanchuan Commandery was established for the first time. Lü Buwei became Chancellor. Took Eastern Zhou.
Han: Qin took our Chenggao and Xingyang.
Chu: Chu destroyed Lu; Duke Qing was moved to Bian, became a commoner, and the sacrifices were cut off.

div.head: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses
div.p: Hereditary House of the Duke of Zhou of Lu: In the twenty-fourth year, King Kaolie of Chu attacked and destroyed Lu. Duke Qing fled and was moved to an outlying settlement; he became a commoner, and Lu's sacrifices were cut off. Duke Qing died at Ke.
From the Duke of Zhou to Duke Qing, Lu had thirty-four generations in all.
Hereditary House of Duke Shao of Yan: In the sixth year, Qin destroyed Eastern Zhou and established Sanchuan Commandery.
Hereditary House of Zhao: In the seventeenth year, the Acting Chancellor and great general Lord Wuxiang attacked Yan and besieged its capital.
Hereditary House of Han: In the twenty-fourth year, Qin took our Chenggao and Xingyang.
Hereditary House of Tian Jingzhong Wan: In the sixteenth year, Qin destroyed Zhou. Queen Jun died.

div.head: Shiji IV: Biographies
div.p: Biography of Lord Chunshen: In the fourteenth year of Lord Chunshen's chancellorship, King Zhuangxiang of Qin came to the throne; he made Lü Buwei Chancellor and enfeoffed him as Marquis Wenxin. Took Eastern Zhou.

div.head: Shiji V: Biographies
div.p: Biography of Lü Buwei: In the first year of King Zhuangxiang, he made Lü Buwei Chancellor, enfeoffed him as Marquis Wenxin, and gave him Luoyang in Henan, a hundred thousand households, as his fief.

Biography of Meng Tian: Meng Tian's forebears were men of Qi. Tian's grandfather Meng Ao came from Qi to serve King Zhao of Qin, and rose in office to Senior Minister. In the first year of King Zhuangxiang of Qin, Meng Ao was a general of Qin; he attacked Han, took Chenggao and Xingyang, and set up Sanchuan Commandery.

div.head: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I
div.p: Marquis Chunping served as Chancellor of State of Zhao.

Analysis: A number of pi blades of Marquis Chunping have been excavated in China, ten of them inscribed "seventeenth year, Chancellor of State Marquis Chunping". Scholars infer that the "seventeenth year" is the earliest year known, but when Marquis Chunping began to serve as Chancellor of State the histories do not record; and moreover Zhao's Chancellors of State were presumably more than one.

div.head: Other ancient works (histories)
div.p: Analysis: Chu annexed Langya and moved King Qin of Yue to Wu.
King Goujian of Yue destroyed Wu and became hegemon in 473 BC; the state of Yue perished after 224 years of hegemony, which gives −473 + 224 = 249 BC
Yuejueshu, Outer Tradition, Record of the Lands:

From King Futan of Yue back to Wuyu is remote and far off, and the generations cannot be recorded. Futan's son was Yunchang. Yunchang's son was Goujian, who was a great hegemon and styled himself king; he moved to Langya and made it his capital. Goujian's son Yuyi was hegemon in his time. Yuyi's son Ziweng was hegemon in his time. Ziweng's son Buyang was hegemon in his time. Buyang's son Wujiang was hegemon in his time; he attacked Chu, and King Wei destroyed Wujiang. Wujiang's son Zhihou set himself up without warrant as chieftain. Zhihou's son Zun was chieftain in his time. Zun's son Qin lost his people; Chu attacked him and he fled to the southern hills. From Qin back to Goujian, eight lords in all, had their capital at Langya for two hundred and twenty-four years. From Wujiang upward they were hegemons and styled themselves king; from Zhihou downward they were weak and were styled chieftains.
Wu Yue Chunqiu (Outer Tradition of Goujian's Attack on Wu, chapter ten)

In the winter of the twenty-seventh year, Goujian lay ill and was about to die, and said to the Heir Apparent Xingyi: "I, descended from Yu, inheriting the virtue of Yuanchang, blessed by the protection of Heaven's spirits and the favour of the gods, from the land of poor and remote Yue, with Chu as my vanguard, broke the shields and spears of the King of Wu. I crossed the Jiang and forded the Huai, passed through the lands of Jin and Qi, and my merit and virtue stood towering. Having brought myself to this, can one fail to take warning? The heirs of a hegemon find it hard to stand for long; be careful of it!" Then he died.

Xingyi came to the throne and died after one year; his son was Weng. Weng died; his son was Buyang. Buyang died; his son was Wuqiang. Qiang died; his son was Yu. Yu died; his son was Zun. Zun died; his son was Qin. From Goujian down to Qin there were eight rulers, all styled hegemon, over two hundred and twenty-four years in all; Qin lost all his people, left Langya and moved to Wu.

From the Yellow Emperor to Shaokang were ten generations; from Yu's receiving the abdication to Shaokang's accession were six generations, one hundred and forty-four years; from Shaokang back to Zhuanxu's accession, four hundred and twenty-four years.

Yellow Emperor → Changyi → Zhuanxu → Gun → Yu → Qi → Taikang → Zhonglu → Xiang → Shaokang → Wuyu → Wuren (ten generations from Wuyu) → Wuyi → Futan → Yuanchang → Goujian → Xingyi → Bushou → Buyang → Wuqiang → Lu Mu Liu, who had Duke You as his name; kings and marquises styled themselves lords → Zun → Qin, who lost Langya and was destroyed by Chu.

From Goujian to King Qin, eight rulers, hegemons for two hundred and twenty-four years. From Wuyu's first enfeoffment in Yue to Yushan's return and the emptying and extinction of the state of Yue, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-two years in all.
In the Xu Hanshu, Treatise on Commanderies and Kingdoms IV, Liu Zhao notes under the entry "An County, Wu Commandery":
The Yuejue says: there is the Xicen tomb, set up by Kai, grandson of the King of Yue, to guard against Lord Chunshen; he had his son hold it, and when the son died he was buried within the Fortress.

Lord Chunshen was enfeoffed in Jiangdong in 248 BC (Shiji, Biography of Lord Chunshen). From this it can be known that in the middle of the third century BC there were still Yue forces in the Jiangsu–Zhejiang region that did not submit to Chu.

The two experts told the reporter that the ancient walled site at Jiulongkou on Jinpingshan, Lianyungang, which archaeologists call the tailings-dam site, had never before been connected with the place to which the King of Yue moved his capital. By survey on the ground they found the site to be an ancient walled city about ten li in circumference. The city is ringed by hills on three sides and faces the sea on the east. Its interior has been filled by the waste sand of the phosphate mine to the left of Jinpingshan, forming an accumulation of sand more than ten li round and some twenty metres deep. A raised terrace of the period, now exposed in the middle of the city, survives, about 300 metres from north to south and some 150 metres from east to west. On this terrace archaeologists collected a great many pottery sherds and fragments of vessels in the Yue style, all identified on examination as stamped hard pottery of the late Spring and Autumn and early Warring States periods, which confirmed that these remains belong to Yue. The experts then found in Du You's Tongdian of the Tang the basis for Jinpingshan's other name, Langyashan. According to the historical records, before the Qin dynasty was founded Jinpingshan was called Qushan, also Langyashan. In the time of the First Emperor of Qin it was made Qu County, and in his thirty-fifth year (212 BC) a stone was set up there as Qin's eastern gate. In his twenty-eighth year the First Emperor also built the Langya Terrace in Shandong, to answer to the Langya settlement. Zhang Zhili and Peng Yun hold that, with the changes of place-names, the name Langyashan gradually fell out of use, and many people have therefore mistaken the place to which King Goujian of Yue moved his capital, Langyashan at Lianyungang, for the Langyashan of Jiaonan city in the Qingdao region of Shandong.
